vignette:
She remembers the exact sound of the monitor’s alarm—a high, flat beep that seemed to stretch time. It was three in the morning, and her son, then eight, lay febrile and pale in a hospital bed. The doctors said it was a rare, aggressive leukemia. She had known the word from her pharmacology textbooks, but it had been abstract, a set of metabolic pathways and side effects. Now it was the weight of his hand in hers, the way his veins collapsed under the tape.

Those first weeks, she stopped working. She lived in the hospital chapel, in the waiting room, in the narrow space between his bed and the IV pole. She learned the rhythms of the nurses’ shifts, the smell of antiseptic and overcooked chicken broth. She kept a notebook—not of prayers, but of drug doses, blood counts, attending physicians’ names. She would correct a resident on the interaction between the antifungal and the chemotherapy, her voice flat, professional. Inside, she was screaming. Every time he vomited, she felt her own stomach clench. Every time his platelets dropped, a cold thumb pressed on her throat.

He survived. The remission came slowly, then all at once, like a door opening. But the door never fully shut. She went back to work at the pharmacy six months after his last infusion. She still wears her white coat, still counts tablets, still checks for interactions. But now, when a mother brings in a child’s antibiotic, she feels her pulse quicken. The child’s cough sounds wrong. The mother’s tired eyes look too familiar. She has to excuse herself to the back room, press her palms against the cold steel of the refrigerator door until the panic subsides. Her boss thinks she has a stomach condition. She lets him.

At home, her son is now sixteen, tall and healthy, with a scar on his chest where the central line used to be. He plays soccer. He argues about homework. He does not remember much from those months, only the taste of ice cream and the way she never left. She does not tell him that she still sleeps with the light on, that she checks his breathing three times a night. She has not had a full night’s rest in eight years. When he has a cold, she calls in sick to work and sits in his doorway, watching his chest rise and fall, counting seconds between breaths. He thinks she is overprotective. He does not know about the nightmares—the ones where his fever spikes to 107, where the monitor flatlines, where she wakes with her own scream caught in her throat.

She is single. There was a brief relationship a few years after his recovery, a kind man who sold medical equipment. He asked why she flinched when he touched her shoulder. She said she was tired. He did not ask again. She finds intimacy exhausting—the risk of another person seeing the raw edge, the way she startles at a car backfiring or a dropped tray. Her social life is the pharmacy counter, the rhythm of prescription bottles, the safe structure of medication counseling. She knows her patients’ names, their diagnoses, their medications. It is a world she can predict.

Today, she stood behind the counter and watched a young father pick up a bottle of liquid Tylenol. His hands were shaking. His daughter had a fever. He asked her, twice, if the dose was correct. She wanted to grab his arm, to say, *Take her to the ER. Do not wait. Do not think it will pass.* But she just smiled, repeated the dose, handed him the bag. When he left, she felt a wave of dizziness, as if the floor had tilted. She went to the break room, locked the door, and sat on the floor with her head between her knees. She did not cry. She has not cried in years. The tears are somewhere deep, behind the sternum, in the same place the fear lives.

She knows the PCL-5 she filled out in the waiting room of a clinic she visited once, a month ago. She scored a 42. She knows what that means. But she does not know how to tell the story without the words catching in her throat. So she keeps working. She keeps counting. She keeps watching his breath.
